text: Your bicep is a lever. And mechanically, it's losing.
Take the arm apart like a machine. Upper arm: the frame. Forearm: a beam. Elbow: the pivot.
The biceps is the actuator. Its tendon anchors just four centimeters from the elbow.
The dumbbell sits thirty five centimeters out. Pivot, effort, load: a third class lever.
Balance the torques. Ten kilos is ninety eight newtons. At thirty five centimeters: thirty four newton meters.
With only four centimeters of leverage, the biceps must pull about eight hundred sixty newtons. Nearly nine times the weight.
Real arms run seven to ten times. So why build it this badly?
Speed. Shorten the muscle one centimeter, and the hand swings almost nine. Small actuator, huge range of motion.
And the load changes through the curl. Arm straight down, almost no torque.
At ninety degrees, the forearm is level. The lever arm is longest. That's the sticking point.
Curl past it, and the torque drops again.
So every rep, your biceps pulls about nine times what you're holding.
What should we take apart next?
Congrats! You've discovered the lever in your arm.
